L46: Large language models are zero-shot time series forecasters (2023) has demonstrated that LLMs can perform time series forecasting by encoding values as text tokens and predicting future values without domain-specific tuning Gruver et al. (Large language models are zero-shot time series forecasters (2023)).Liu et al.
L50: An alternative to manual tokenization is to encode time series into embeddings that capture time series information, using a time series encoder as presented by Nie et al. (cite15†A time series is worth 64 words: Long-term forecasting with transformers (2023)†openreview.net ). These embeddings can be input into a transformer directly or concatenated with text embeddings (softprompting) Chow et al. (cite18†Towards time series reasoning with llms (2024) ); Nie et al.
L51: (cite15†A time series is worth 64 words: Long-term forecasting with transformers (2023)†openreview.net ); Pillai et al. (cite16†Time2lang: Bridging time-series foundation models and large language models for health sensing beyond prompting (2025) ); Ye et al. (cite17†Medualtime: A dual-adapter language model for medical time series-text multimodal learning (2025) ). Pillai et al.
L54: (cite14†Sensorllm: Human-intuitive alignment of multivariate sensor data with llms for activity recognition (2025) ) integrate sensor and text embeddings in two stages: First, they generate a caption-like summary of the time series for free-form output; Second, they classify the data via a projection head, therefore restricting free from output. Chow et al. (cite18†Towards time series reasoning with llms (2024) ) interleave time series tokens with text tokens in the LLM input, enabling free-form text reasoning.
L56: Few studies use cross-attention to integrate time series into LLMs. Zhang et al. (cite24†Sensorlm: Learning the language of wearable sensors (2025) ) apply cross-attention between a time series encoder and a text encoder, aligned with contrastive loss, to extract statistical summaries (e.g., mean, max) from a single sensor. They train a new sensor encoder, text encoder, and multimodal text decoder, rather than adapting a pretrained LLM Zhang et al.
L59: We present two architectures for TSLMs, OpenTSLM-Soft Prompting (SP) (3.2 Soft-prompting architecture (OpenTSLM-SP) ‣ 3 Methods ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data and OpenTSLM-Flamingo (3.3 Cross-attention architecture (OpenTSLM-Flamingo) ‣ 3 Methods ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data).
L60: To support multiple time-series inputs, we design a prompt format that interleaves sensor data with accompanying textual descriptions (e.g., “Data from Sensor X over Y days:” followed by the data representation). Figure 1 ‣ 3 Methods ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data illustrates our approach.
L61: Figure 1: Overview of Text–Time-Series LLMs with support for multiple time-series inputs.
L62: ### 3.1 Time-Series encoder
L63: Both OpenTSLM architectures use a time series encoder inspired by Nie et al. (cite15†A time series is worth 64 words: Long-term forecasting with transformers (2023)†openreview.net ). It consists of a Patchencoder, followed by either a TransformerEncoder for OpenTSLM-SP or a PerceiverResampler for OpenTSLM-Flamingo (inspired by Alayrac et al. (cite20†Flamingo: a visual language model for few-shot learning (2022) ); Awadalla et al.
L64: (cite26†Openflamingo: An open-source framework for training large autoregressive vision-language models (2023) )). We divide an input time series $x\in\mathbb{R}^{L}$ into non-overlapping patches of size $p$, yielding $N=L/p$ patches. Each patch is then transformed into an embedding vector using a 1D convolution and added with a positional encoding Nie et al. (cite15†A time series is worth 64 words: Long-term forecasting with transformers (2023)†openreview.net )
L67: Sections 3.2 Soft-prompting architecture (OpenTSLM-SP) ‣ 3 Methods ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data and  3.3 Cross-attention architecture (OpenTSLM-Flamingo) ‣ 3 Methods ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data).
L68: ##### Preserving scale and temporal information
L69: 
L70: The PatchEncoder expects inputs normalized to $x\in[-1,1]$. Since raw time series differ in scale and resolution across modalities depending on the sensor, we preserve scale and temporal context by adding the original mean, standard deviation, and time scale to the textual description. For example:
L71: 
L72: > This is heart-rate data over 24 hours sampled at 50 Hz with mean=61 and std=12.
L74: OpenTSLM-SP has three components: (1) a time series encoder that transforms raw data into patch embeddings, (2) a projection layer mapping embeddings to the LLM hidden space, (3) a pretrained LLM, fine-tuned using LoRA adapters Hu et al. (cite27†Lora: Low-rank adaptation of large language models (2021) ) Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Soft-prompting architecture (OpenTSLM-SP) ‣ 3 Methods ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data illustrates the architecture.
L76: ##### Projecting Time-Series Tokens to Text Tokens
L77: 
L78: We apply the patch embeddings to a transformer encoder and subsequently project the resulting tokens with an multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to align them with the embedding space of dimension $d_{\text{llm}}$, corresponding to the hidden size of the language model, following Nie et al. (cite15†A time series is worth 64 words: Long-term forecasting with transformers (2023)†openreview.net ) and Chow et al. (cite18†Towards time series reasoning with llms (2024) ).
L92: Figure 3 ‣ Architecture Overview ‣ 3.3 Cross-attention architecture (OpenTSLM-Flamingo) ‣ 3 Methods ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data visualizes the architecture.
L122: Time-Series Captioning (M4-Captions) We generate pseudo-labeled captions using ChatGPT, prompted with plots of time series of the M4 dataset Makridakis et al. (cite29†The m4 competition: 100,000 time series and 61 forecasting methods (2020)†api.semanticscholar.org ) (see A.5.1 M4 time-series captioning ‣ A.5 Further examples for rationales generated by OpenTSLM models ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data).
L124: Further details are provided in A.2 Generation of multivariate time series CoT datasets ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data.
L129: See A.2.1 Human Activity Recogniton (HAR) CoT ‣ A.2 Generation of multivariate time series CoT datasets ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data for detailed description.
L131: Sleep-CoT Based on SleepEDF Kemp et al. (cite38†Analysis of a sleep-dependent neuronal feedback loop: the slow-wave microcontinuity of the eeg (2000)†api.semanticscholar.org ); Goldberger et al. (Components of a new research resource for complex physiologic signals (2000)), using 30s electroencephalogram (EEG) segments for sleep staging. Following prior work Chow et al. (cite18†Towards time series reasoning with llms (2024) ); Pouliou et al.
L132: (cite39†A new approach for sleep stage identification combining hidden markov models and eeg signal processing (2025)†doi.org ), Non-rapid eye movement (REM) stages 3 and 4 are merged, yielding five classes: Wake, REM, Non-REM 1, Non-REM 2, Non-REM 3.
L133: See A.2.2 Sleep Stage Classification Chain-of-Thought (SleepEDF-CoT) ‣ A.2 Generation of multivariate time series CoT datasets ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data for details.
L134:   * •
L135: ECG-QA-CoT Based on ECG-QA Oh et al. (Ecg-qa: A comprehensive question answering dataset combined with electrocardiogram (2023)), which provides 12-lead 10s ECGs and clinical context, we excluded comparison questions, retaining 42/70 templates.
L136: This yielded 3,138 unique questions across 240k samples (see A.2.3 Electrocardiogram Question Answering Chain-of-Thought (ECG-QA-CoT) ‣ A.2 Generation of multivariate time series CoT datasets ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data).
L137: All datasets are split into 80/10/10 train/validation/test sets. Table 3 ‣ A.1 Training details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data in  A.1 Training details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data summarizes number of samples in the datasets, number of time series and lengths.
L138: ##### Training objective
L139: In all stages, we frame the task as an autoregressive language modeling problem. During training and evaluation, the model is prompted to generate outputs in a structured format, consisting of a free-form rationale followed by the final prediction: ‘‘<reasoning> Answer: <final answer>’’.
L140: Formally, the loss is defined by 8 ‣ Training objective ‣ 4.1 Multi-Stage Curriculum Learning – Teaching LLMs Time Series ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data, where $\mathbf{Z}_{\text{ts}}$ are the
L141:  | $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}}=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log P(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},\mathbf{x}_{1:t},\mathbf{Z}_{\text{ts}};\Theta)$$  |  | (8)
L142: 
L143: time-series features, and $\Theta$ the learnable weights, i.e., the TimeSeriesEncoder, MLP, and LoRA in OpenTSLM-SoftPrompt, and TimeSeriesEncoder and cross-attention in OpenTSLM-Flamingo.
L144: ### 4.2 Baselines
L145: 
L146: We compare OpenTSLM against three baselines using the same open-weight LLMs, i.e., Llama-3.2(1B, 3B) and Gemma3 (270M, 1B-PT), and additionally GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06).
L147: 
L148:   1. 1.
L149: 
L150: Tokenized time-series: Using the open-source code provided by Gruver et al. (Large language models are zero-shot time series forecasters (2023)), we tokenize time series into text inputs and report zero-shot performance on the test set.
L151: 
L152:   2. 2.
L153: Tokenized finetuned: Same as 1. (excluding GPT-4o), but finetuned with LoRA Hu et al. (cite27†Lora: Low-rank adaptation of large language models (2021) ) on the training set. We choose best model by validation loss, and report performance on test set.
L154: 
L155:   3. 3.

L158:

L161: ### 4.3 Quantitative results on time-series classification
L162: 
L163: We present performance on the test splits of TSQA, HAR-CoT, Sleep-CoT, and ECG-QA-CoT and report macro-F1 score and accuracy in Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Quantitative results on time-series classification ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data.

L188: OpenTSLM models achieve the highest performance across benchmarks, while most tokenized text-only baselines fail to produce valid outputs, not answering in the expected template but merely repeating inputs or starting to count (see A.4 Example of Baselines failing to produce meaningful output ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data), resulting in 0.00 F1 on HAR for all models except for GPT-4o (2.95).
L193: ### 4.4 Evaluation of memory use during training
L194: 
L195: We evaluate peak VRAM usage during training for both OpenTSLM variants. Figure 4 ‣ 4.4 Evaluation of memory use during training ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data summarizes peak VRAM on TSQA, HAR–CoT, SleepEDF–CoT, and ECG–QA–CoT.
L196: 
L197: Figure 4: VRAM memory usage in training across datasets.
L199: To further investigate memory scaling, we train models on a simulated dataset (see A.7.2 Memory usage for Simulation Data ‣ A.7 Evaluation of memory consumption ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data) with random inputs of shape $(N\times L)$, where $N$ is the number of time series processed concurrently and $L$ the sequence length.
L200: We report max VRAM usage in Figure 5 ‣ 4.4 Evaluation of memory use during training ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data (exact values are available in Table 11 ‣ Simulation dataset generation. ‣ A.7.2 Memory usage for Simulation Data ‣ A.7 Evaluation of memory consumption ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data).
L201: Figure 5: VRAM usage vs. total time-series size $N\times L$ (number of series × length)
L202: VRAM for OpenTSLM-Flamingo effectively stays constant as $N$ increases from 1 to 5 and $L$ from 10 to 10,000 (e.g., Llama-1B $\approx$20.4–21.0 GB; Llama-3B $\approx$60.7–61.1 GB; Gemma-270M $\approx$5.7–6.4 GB; Gemma-1B $\approx$15.4–15.6 GB).
L203: By contrast, SoftPrompt scales with both $N$ and $L$ (see Figure 5 ‣ 4.4 Evaluation of memory use during training ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data in A.7.2 Memory usage for Simulation Data ‣ A.7 Evaluation of memory consumption ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data): for Llama-1B, VRAM rises from $\sim$2.6 GB at $L{=}10,N{=}1$ to $\sim$29.5 GB at $L{=}10{,}000,N{=}1$ and exceeds memory at $L{=}10{,}000,N{\geq}3$; Llama-3B shows a similar pattern (6.3 GB $\rightarrow$ 42.7 GB at $N{=}1$, OOM by $N{\geq}3$).
L204: Gemma-270M and Gemma-1B reach up to $\sim$118 GB and $\sim$165 GB, respectively, at $L{=}10{,}000,N{=}5$.
L205: ### 4.5 Qualitative results and expert evaluation of ECG rationales
L206: Both OpenTSLM variants remain text models, trained to generate rationales for classification rather than outputting only a class label.
L207: 6(a) ‣ Figure 6 ‣ 4.5 Qualitative results and expert evaluation of ECG rationales ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data shows example rationales for human activity recognition, 6(b) ‣ Figure 6 ‣ 4.5 Qualitative results and expert evaluation of ECG rationales ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data for ECG-QA, and 6(c) ‣ Figure 6 ‣ 4.5 Qualitative results and expert evaluation of ECG rationales ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data for sleep staging.
L208: 6(d) ‣ Figure 6 ‣ 4.5 Qualitative results and expert evaluation of ECG rationales ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data shows time series captioning on M4 data.

More examples are provided in A.5 Further examples for rationales generated by OpenTSLM models ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data.
L218: To evaluate the quality of model rationales, we conducted an expert review with five cardiologists from Stanford Hospital on rationales generated by OpenTSLM-Flamingo-Llama3.2-3B (best model) for ECG-QA.
L219: 
L220: (a) Performance by Area

L224: Figure 7: Qualitative evaluation of CoT rationales and inter-reviewer agreement patterns.
L225: We randomly sampled two examples per template (84 total), each reviewed by at least two cardiologists. Evaluation followed a rubric derived from the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Clinical Competence Statement on ECGs Pangaro (cite40†A new vocabulary and other innovations for improving descriptive in-training evaluations (1999)†doi.org ); Committee Members et al.
L226: (cite41†Acc/aha clinical competence statement on electrocardiography and ambulatory electrocardiography (2001)†www.ahajournals.org ) and based on the RIME (“Reporter–Interpreter–Manager–Educator”) framework Pangaro (cite40†A new vocabulary and other innovations for improving descriptive in-training evaluations (1999)†doi.org ) (see A.6 ECG Evaluation Rubric ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data), assessing whether the model: (1) correctly identified relevant ECG features; (2) appropriately connected them to the final answer; (3) incorporated patient context (age, artifacts, …).
L227: Overall, the model gave a correct or partially correct ECG interpretation in 92.9% of cases, spanning ECG recognition, reasoning, and contextualization.
L228: OpenTSLM showed strongest performance in clinical context integration (85.1% positive) compared to ECG pattern recognition (65.5% positive) and clinical reasoning (62.5% positive) (7(a) ‣ Figure 7 ‣ 4.5 Qualitative results and expert evaluation of ECG rationales ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data).
L229: Assessment patterns varied notably across reviewers, with some reviewers consistently more favorable across all evaluation areas (7(b) ‣ Figure 7 ‣ 4.5 Qualitative results and expert evaluation of ECG rationales ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data). Reviewer disagreement was most common for clinical reasoning, where moderate disagreements were observed between adjacent assessment categories.
L230: Complete disagreements between positive and negative assessments were relatively rare across all areas (Figure 17 ‣ A.6.2 Reviewer disagreement patterns ‣ A.6 ECG Evaluation Rubric ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data in Appendix A.6 ECG Evaluation Rubric ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data).
L231: ## 5 Discussion
L232: All OpenTSLM models consistently outperform baselines. Text-only models often fail to follow the answer template and thus perform at or below chance (4.1 Multi-Stage Curriculum Learning – Teaching LLMs Time Series ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data). Finetuned baselines improve substantially on HAR-CoT (60.44% F1 vs. 0% for Llama-3.2-1B) but only slightly on Sleep-CoT (9.05 vs. 2.14).
L233: ECG-QA finetuning was infeasible due to high VRAM demands (80k tokens require >100GB per sample). OpenTSLM-SoftPrompt performs best on shorter sequences (Sleep-CoT, TSQA) but becomes impractical as VRAM requirements grow with sequence length (>180GB in simulations with 10,000-length series). With softprompting, smaller models like Gemma-3 270M and 1B quickly exhaust their context and underperform.
L234: In contrast, OpenTSLM-Flamingo sustains stable memory across sequence lengths and series (up to 60GB for Llama-3.2-3B with five 10,000-length series). This allows even tiny models, such as Gemma-270M, to deliver strong results, highlighting the efficiency of cross-attention for treating time series as a native modality.

L180: # OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data
L181: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for interpreting multimodal data (e.g., images, audio, text), often surpassing specialized models. In medicine, they hold particular promise for synthesizing large volumes of clinical information into actionable insights and patient-facing digital health applications. Yet, a major limitation remains their inability to handle time series data.
L182: To overcome this gap, we present OpenTSLM, a family of Time Series Language Models (TSLMs) created by integrating time series as a native modality to pretrained Large Language Models, enabling natural-language prompting and reasoning over multiple time series of any length [...] cite93†🔗 Read the full paper†doi.org L183: ## Examples
L184: 
L185: OpenTSLM models can reason over multiple time series of any length at once, generating findings, captions, and rationales in natural language. We tested these models across a wide range of tasks spanning Human Activity Recognition (HAR) from 3-axis acceleration data, sleep staging from EEG readings, 12-lead ECG question answering, and time series captioning. Some examples are shown below, more are available in the paper.
L186: 
L187: ## Installation
L188: 
L189:     pip install opentslm
L190: ## LLM Setup
L191: 
L192: OpenTSLM is designed to work with Llama and Gemma models, with Llama 3.2 1B as the default. These models are stored in Hugging Face repositories which may require access permissions. Follow these steps to gain access and download:
L193:   1. Request Access (for Llama models)
L194: Visit the Llama model repository (e.g., cite94†https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B†huggingface.co ) or Gemma models repository (cite95†https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-3-270m†huggingface.co ) and request access from Meta.
L195: 
L196:   2. Authenticate with Hugging Face
L197: Log in to your Hugging Face account and configure the CLI:
L198: 
L199:     huggingface-cli login
L200: 
L201:   3. Create an API Token
L202:      * Go to your Hugging Face settings: cite96†https://huggingface.co/settings/tokens†huggingface.co L203:      * Generate a new token with `read` scope.
L204:      * Copy the token for CLI login.
L205: ### Supported Models
L206: 
L207: OpenTSLM has been tested and works with the following models:
L208: 
L209: Llama Models:
L210: 
L211:   * meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B (default)
L212:   * meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B
L213: 
L214: Gemma Models:
L215: 
L216:   * google/gemma-3-270m
L217:   * google/gemma-3-1b-pt
L218: 
L219: Other variants may work but have not been extensively tested.
L220: ## 🤗 Quickstart with pretrained models on HuggingFace
L221: 
L222: A factory class called `OpenTSLM` for easily loading pre-trained models from Hugging Face Hub. The `load_pretrained` method automatically detects the model type and returns the appropriate model instance.
L223: There are cite97†demo scripts available which use the following minimal code. If you want to create your own applications, create a new file in this repo folder and use the following code as start:
L224: 
L225:     from opentslm import OpenTSLM
L226:     from opentslm.time_series_datasets.TSQADataset import TSQADataset
L227:     from opentslm.time_series_datasets.util import extend_time_series_to_match_patch_size_and_aggregate
L228:     from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
L229:     from opentslm.model_config import PATCH_SIZE
L230:     REPO_ID = "OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-1b-tsqa-sp"
L231: 
L232:     # Use CPU or CUDA for inference. MPS does NOT work for pretrained HF checkpoints.
L233:     model = OpenTSLM.load_pretrained(REPO_ID, device="cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
L234:     test_dataset = TSQADataset("test", EOS_TOKEN=model.get_eos_token())
L235: 
L236:     test_loader = DataLoader(
L237:         test_dataset,
L238:         shuffle=False,
L239:         batch_size=1,
L240:         collate_fn=lambda batch: extend_time_series_to_match_patch_size_and_aggregate(
L241:              batch, patch_size=PATCH_SIZE
L242:         ),
L243:     )
L244: 
L245:     for i, batch in enumerate(test_loader):
L246:         predictions = model.generate(batch, max_new_tokens=200)
L247:         for sample, pred in zip(batch, predictions):
L248:              print("Question:", sample.get("pre_prompt", "N/A"))
L249:              print("Answer:", sample.get("answer", "N/A"))
L250:              print("Output:", pred)
L251:         if i >= 4:
L252:              break
L253: ## Building and finetuning your own models
L254: To run the demos and use finetuning scripts clone the repository and set up all dependencies. We recommend using cite98†uv†docs.astral.sh to set up the environment, but you can also use pip:
L255: 
L256:     git clone https://github.com/OpenTSLM/OpenTSLM.git
L257: 
L258: 
L259:     # uv environment management (recommended). Installs uv if it does not exist and creates the virtual environment
L260:     command uv > /dev/null || curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
L261:     uv sync --all-groups
L262:     source .venv/bin/activate
L263: 
L264: 
L265:     # or alternatively install via pip:
L266:     pip install -r requirements.txt
L267: ### HuggingFace Demo Scripts
L268: 
L269: We provide ready-to-use demo scripts in the `demo/huggingface/` directory that demonstrate how to load pretrained models from HuggingFace Hub and run inference on the evaluation sets for each task:
L270:   * `01_test_hf_tsqa.py` - Test TSQA (Time Series Question Answering) models
L271:   * `02_test_hf_m4.py` - Test M4 (Time Series Captioning) models
L272:   * `03_test_hf_har_cot.py` - Test HAR CoT (Human Activity Recognition Chain-of-Thought) models
L273:   * `04_test_hf_sleep_cot.py` - Test Sleep CoT (Sleep Stage Classification) models
L274:   * `05_test_hf_ecg_qa_cot.py` - Test ECG QA CoT (ECG Question Answering) models
L275: 
L276: Each script:
L277:   1. Downloads the model checkpoint from HuggingFace Hub automatically (change repo id as neededs)
L278:   2. Loads the corresponding test dataset
L279:   3. Runs inference on the evaluation set
L280:   4. Prints model outputs with sample information
L281: 
L282: Note: The scripts above use the OpenTSLM-SP models except for ECG-QA, as they require less VRAM and should run on most hardware. Change the model checkpoints as needed in each file.
L283: Usage:
L284: 
L285:     # Run any of the demo scripts
L286:     python demo/huggingface/01_test_hf_tsqa.py
L287:     python demo/huggingface/02_test_hf_m4.py
L288:     python demo/huggingface/03_test_hf_har_cot.py
L289:     python demo/huggingface/04_test_hf_sleep_cot.py
L290:     python demo/huggingface/05_test_hf_ecg_qa_cot.py
L291: 
L292: Customizing the model:
L293: Edit the `REPO_ID` variable at the top of each script to test different model variants. For example:
L294: 
L295:     # In 01_test_hf_tsqa.py
L296:     REPO_ID = "OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-1b-tsqa-sp"  # Soft Prompt model
L297:     # or
L298:     REPO_ID = "OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-1b-tsqa-flamingo"  # Flamingo model
L299: 
L300: Available models on HuggingFace:
L301: 
L302: All pretrained models are available under the `OpenTSLM` organization on HuggingFace Hub. Model names follow the pattern:
L303:   * `OpenTSLM/{base_model}-{dataset}-{model_type}`
L304:     * `base_model`: `llama-3.2-1b`, `llama-3.2-3b`, `gemma-3-1b-pt`, `gemma-3-270m`
L305:     * `dataset`: `tsqa`, `m4`, `har`, `sleep`, `ecg`
L306:     * `model_type`: `sp` (Soft Prompt) or `flamingo` (Flamingo)
L307: 
L308: Example: `OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-1b-ecg-flamingo`
L309: ## Training: Multi-stage training (Curriculum)
L310: 
L311: OpenTSLM uses curriculum learning with progressive training stages:
L312: ### Training Stages
L313: 
L314:   1. Stage 1 (MCQ): Multiple choice questions on time series data (TSQA dataset)
L315:   2. Stage 2 (Captioning): Generate detailed captions for time series (M4 dataset)
L316:   3. Stage 3 (CoT): Chain-of-thought reasoning on human activity recognition (HAR dataset)
L317:   4. Stage 4 (Sleep CoT): Chain-of-thought reasoning on sleep stage classification (SleepEDF dataset)
L318:   5. Stage 5 (ECG CoT): Chain-of-thought reasoning on ECG question answering (ECG QA dataset)
L319: > ⚠️ MPS/CUDA Compatibility Warning:
L320: >
L321: > If you are using Apple's MPS (Metal Performance Shaders) backend (e.g., on Mac with Apple Silicon), you may encounter issues with training or inference. Checkpoints trained with CUDA (NVIDIA GPUs) may not yield good results or may not be fully compatible when loaded and run on MPS. For best results, use the same device type (CUDA or MPS) for both training and inference. CUDA is preferred in general.
L322: ### Quick Start
L323: 
L324:     # Run full curriculum with OpenTSLMFlamingo
L325:     python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMSP
L326: 
L327:     # Run full curriculum with OpenTSLMSP
L328:     python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo
L329: 
L330:     # Run specific stages
L331:     python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage1_mcq
L332:     python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage2_captioning
L333:     python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage3_cot
L334:     python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage4_sleep_cot
L335:     python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage5_ecg_cot
L336: 
L337:     # Run multiple stages
L338:     python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage1_mcq stage2_captioning stage3_cot
L339: 
L340:     # Specify device
L341:     python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --device cuda
L342: 
L343:     # Use different models
L344:     python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --llm_id meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B
L345:     python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --llm_id google/gemma-3-270m
L346: 
L347:     # Run only evaluation
L348:     python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --eval_only
L349: ### Command Line Arguments
L350:   * `--model`: Model type (`OpenTSLMSP` or `OpenTSLMFlamingo`)
L351:   * `--stages`: Stages to run (any combination of: `stage1_mcq`, `stage2_captioning`, `stage3_cot`, `stage4_sleep_cot`, `stage5_ecg_cot`)

L354:   * `--llm_id`: Model ID (default: `meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B`, supports Llama and Gemma models)
L355:   * `--batch_size`: Batch size for training
L356:   * `--gradient_checkpointing`: Enable gradient checkpointing for memory efficiency
L357:   * `--verbose`: Enable verbose logging

    def _calculate_accuracy(
        self, predictions: List[str], gold_answers: List[str]
    ) -> float:
        """Calculate accuracy for MCQ tasks."""
        correct = 0
        total = len(predictions)

        for pred, gold in zip(predictions, gold_answers):
            # Clean up predictions and gold answers
            pred_clean = pred.strip()
            gold_clean = gold.strip()

            # Check if gold starts with the cleaned prediction (more robust matching)
            if gold_clean.startswith(pred_clean) or pred_clean == gold_clean:
                correct += 1

        return correct / total if total > 0 else 0.0

    def _evaluate_stage(
        self,
        stage: str,
        test_loader: DataLoader,
        stage_name: str,
        metric_func: Callable = None,
        epoch: int = None,
    ) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Evaluate model on test set for a specific stage."""
        # Enable eval mode for all ranks
        self.model.eval()
        results = []
        test_loss = 0.0

        # Set higher max_tokens for generation during evaluation
        max_new_tokens = 2000

        # Prepare per-rank streaming writer for test predictions
        results_file_rank = os.path.join(
            self.results_dir,
            stage_name,
            "results",
            f"test_predictions_rank_{self.rank if dist.is_initialized() else 0}.jsonl",
        )
        final_results_file = os.path.join(
            self.results_dir, stage_name, "results", "test_predictions.jsonl"
        )
        results_fp = None
        # Ensure directory exists (defensive)
        os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(results_file_rank), exist_ok=True)
        if self.rank == 0:
            print(f"[Eval] rank={self.rank}, world_size={self.world_size}")
            print(f"Saving per-rank test predictions to: {results_file_rank}")
            if dist.is_initialized():
                print(
                    f"Final merged predictions will be saved to: {final_results_file}"
                )
        # Open per-rank file in write mode to start fresh, then append per-sample
        results_fp = open(results_file_rank, "w", encoding="utf-8")
        if not results_fp:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"Failed to open per-rank results file: {results_file_rank}"
            )
        try:
            with torch.no_grad():
                for batch in tqdm(
                    test_loader, desc=f"Evaluating {stage_name}", disable=self.rank != 0
                ):
                    # Generate predictions with higher max_tokens (skip separate loss computation)
                    predictions = self._get_model().generate(
                        batch, max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens
                    )

                    # Collect results
                    for sample, pred in zip(batch, predictions):
                        result = {
                            "pre_prompt": sample["pre_prompt"],
                            "time_series_text": sample["time_series_text"],
                            "post_prompt": sample["post_prompt"],
                            "generated": pred,
                            "gold": sample["answer"],
                        }

                        # Add time series ID for stage2 captioning
                        if stage == "stage2_captioning" and "id" in sample:
                            result["time_series_id"] = sample["id"]

                        # Add template_id and ecg_id for stage5_ecg_cot
                        if stage == "stage5_ecg_cot":
                            if "template_id" in sample:
                                result["template_id"] = sample["template_id"]
                            if "ecg_id" in sample:
                                result["ecg_id"] = sample["ecg_id"]
                            if "correct_answer" in sample:
                                result["correct_answer"] = sample["correct_answer"]
                        results.append(result)
                        # Stream write each result immediately to per-rank file
                        results_fp.write(json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
                        results_fp.flush()
                        try:
                            os.fsync(results_fp.fileno())
                        except Exception:
                            pass
        finally:
            if results_fp is not None:
                results_fp.close()

        # Synchronize all ranks before merging
        if dist.is_initialized():
            dist.barrier()

        # Rank 0 merges per-rank files into final results file
        if (not dist.is_initialized()) or (self.rank == 0):
            try:
                # Overwrite final file each evaluation
                with open(final_results_file, "w", encoding="utf-8") as merged_fp:
                    if dist.is_initialized():
                        num_ranks = self.world_size
                    else:
                        num_ranks = 1
                    for r in range(num_ranks):
                        part_file = os.path.join(
                            self.results_dir,
                            stage_name,
                            "results",
                            f"test_predictions_rank_{r}.jsonl",
                        )
                        if os.path.exists(part_file):
                            with open(part_file, "r", encoding="utf-8") as pf:
                                for line in pf:
                                    merged_fp.write(line)
                if self.rank == 0:
                    print(f"Merged per-rank predictions into: {final_results_file}")
            finally:
                pass
        avg_test_loss = float("nan")
        # Calculate stage-specific metrics
        metrics = {"test_loss": avg_test_loss}
        if epoch is not None:
            metrics["epoch"] = epoch
        if metric_func:
            # Compute metrics on rank 0 after merging, else minimal metrics
            if (not dist.is_initialized()) or (self.rank == 0):
                predictions = []
                gold_answers = []
                # Read from final merged file
                merged_path = final_results_file
                with open(merged_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
                    for line in f:
                        try:
                            obj = json.loads(line)
                            predictions.append(obj.get("generated", ""))
                            gold_answers.append(obj.get("gold", ""))
                        except Exception:
                            continue
                additional_metrics = metric_func(predictions, gold_answers)
                metrics.update(additional_metrics)
        # Save results only on rank 0 (or when not distributed)
        if (not dist.is_initialized()) or (self.rank == 0):
            # Save metrics
            metrics_file = os.path.join(
                self.results_dir, stage_name, "results", "metrics.json"
            )
            with open(metrics_file, "w") as f:
                json.dump(metrics, f, indent=2)

            print(f"✅ {stage_name} evaluation complete:")
            print(f"   Test predictions saved to: {final_results_file}")
            print(f"   Metrics saved to: {metrics_file}")
            print(f"   Max tokens used for generation: {max_new_tokens}")
            for metric, value in metrics.items():
                if isinstance(value, (int, float)):
                    print(f"   {metric}: {value:.4f}")
                else:
                    print(f"   {metric}: {value}")

        # Signal other ranks that evaluation is complete
        if dist.is_initialized():
            dist.barrier()

        return metrics

    def _is_evaluation_completed(self, stage: str) -> bool:
        """Check if evaluation was completed for a stage by looking for test predictions file."""
        test_predictions_file = os.path.join(
            self.results_dir, stage, "results", "test_predictions.jsonl"
        )
        metrics_file = os.path.join(self.results_dir, stage, "results", "metrics.json")

        # Check if both files exist
        if not os.path.exists(test_predictions_file) or not os.path.exists(
            metrics_file
        ):
            return False

        # Also check if metrics file has evaluation results
        try:
            with open(metrics_file, "r") as f:
                metrics = json.load(f)
            return "test_loss" in metrics
        except:
            return False

    def _train_stage(
        self,
        stage_name: str,
        dataset_class,
        num_epochs: int,
        lr_encoder: float,
        lr_projector: float,
        lr_base: float,
        metric_func: Callable = None,
        batch_size: int = None,
        eval_only: bool = False,
        sampler=None,
    ) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Generic training function for any stage."""
        epoch = None
        # Use provided batch_size or default to global BATCH_SIZE
        if batch_size is None:
            batch_size = BATCH_SIZE

        if self.rank == 0:
            print(f"\n🚀 Starting {stage_name} Training with {self.model_type}")
            if eval_only:
                print("🔍 EVAL-ONLY MODE: Skipping training, only running evaluation")
            print("=" * 60)

    def _calculate_accuracy(
        self, predictions: List[str], gold_answers: List[str]
    ) -> float:
        """Calculate accuracy for MCQ tasks."""
        correct = 0
        total = len(predictions)

        for pred, gold in zip(predictions, gold_answers):

            gold_clean = gold.strip()

    def _evaluate_stage(
        self,
        stage: str,
        test_loader: DataLoader,
        stage_name: str,
        metric_func: Callable = None,
        epoch: int = None,
    ) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Evaluate model on test set for a specific stage."""
        # Enable eval mode for all ranks
        self.model.eval()
        results = []
        test_loss = 0.0

        # Set higher max_tokens for generation during evaluation
        max_new_tokens = 2000

        # Prepare per-rank streaming writer for test predictions
        results_file_rank = os.path.join(
            self.results_dir,
            stage_name,
            "results",
            f"test_predictions_rank_{self.rank if dist.is_initialized() else 0}.jsonl",
        )
        final_results_file = os.path.join(
            self.results_dir, stage_name, "results", "test_predictions.jsonl"
        )
        results_fp = None
        # Ensure directory exists (defensive)
        os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(results_file_rank), exist_ok=True)
        if self.rank == 0:
            print(f"[Eval] rank={self.rank}, world_size={self.world_size}")
            print(f"Saving per-rank test predictions to: {results_file_rank}")
            if dist.is_initialized():
                print(
                    f"Final merged predictions will be saved to: {final_results_file}"
                )
        # Open per-rank file in write mode to start fresh, then append per-sample
        results_fp = open(results_file_rank, "w", encoding="utf-8")
        if not results_fp:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"Failed to open per-rank results file: {results_file_rank}"
            )
        try:
            with torch.no_grad():
                for batch in tqdm(
                    test_loader, desc=f"Evaluating {stage_name}", disable=self.rank != 0
                ):
                    # Generate predictions with higher max_tokens (skip separate loss computation)
                    predictions = self._get_model().generate(
                        batch, max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens
                    )

                    # Collect results
                    for sample, pred in zip(batch, predictions):
                        result = {
                            "pre_prompt": sample["pre_prompt"],
                            "time_series_text": sample["time_series_text"],
                            "post_prompt": sample["post_prompt"],
                            "generated": pred,
                            "gold": sample["answer"],
                        }

                        # Add time series ID for stage2 captioning
                        if stage == "stage2_captioning" and "id" in sample:
                            result["time_series_id"] = sample["id"]

                        # Add template_id and ecg_id for stage5_ecg_cot
                        if stage == "stage5_ecg_cot":
                            if "template_id" in sample:
                                result["template_id"] = sample["template_id"]
                            if "ecg_id" in sample:
                                result["ecg_id"] = sample["ecg_id"]
                            if "correct_answer" in sample:
                                result["correct_answer"] = sample["correct_answer"]
                        results.append(result)
                        # Stream write each result immediately to per-rank file
                        results_fp.write(json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
                        results_fp.flush()
                        try:
                            os.fsync(results_fp.fileno())
                        except Exception:
                            pass
        finally:
            if results_fp is not None:
                results_fp.close()

        # Synchronize all ranks before merging
        if dist.is_initialized():
            dist.barrier()

        # Rank 0 merges per-rank files into final results file
        if (not dist.is_initialized()) or (self.rank == 0):
            try:
                # Overwrite final file each evaluation
                with open(final_results_file, "w", encoding="utf-8") as merged_fp:
                    if dist.is_initialized():
                        num_ranks = self.world_size
                    else:
                        num_ranks = 1
                    for r in range(num_ranks):
                        part_file = os.path.join(
                            self.results_dir,
                            stage_name,
                            "results",
                            f"test_predictions_rank_{r}.jsonl",
                        )
                        if os.path.exists(part_file):
                            with open(part_file, "r", encoding="utf-8") as pf:
                                for line in pf:
                                    merged_fp.write(line)
                if self.rank == 0:
                    print(f"Merged per-rank predictions into: {final_results_file}")
            finally:
                pass
        avg_test_loss = float("nan")
        # Calculate stage-specific metrics
        metrics = {"test_loss": avg_test_loss}
        if epoch is not None:
            metrics["epoch"] = epoch
        if metric_func:
            # Compute metrics on rank 0 after merging, else minimal metrics
            if (not dist.is_initialized()) or (self.rank == 0):
                predictions = []
                gold_answers = []
                # Read from final merged file
                merged_path = final_results_file
                with open(merged_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
                    for line in f:
                        try:
                            obj = json.loads(line)
                            predictions.append(obj.get("generated", ""))
                            gold_answers.append(obj.get("gold", ""))
                        except Exception:
                            continue
                additional_metrics = metric_func(predictions, gold_answers)
                metrics.update(additional_metrics)
        # Save results only on rank 0 (or when not distributed)
        if (not dist.is_initialized()) or (self.rank == 0):
            # Save metrics
            metrics_file = os.path.join(
                self.results_dir, stage_name, "results", "metrics.json"
            )
            with open(metrics_file, "w") as f:
                json.dump(metrics, f, indent=2)

            print(f"✅ {stage_name} evaluation complete:")
            print(f"   Test predictions saved to: {final_results_file}")
            print(f"   Metrics saved to: {metrics_file}")
            print(f"   Max tokens used for generation: {max_new_tokens}")
            for metric, value in metrics.items():
                if isinstance(value, (int, float)):
                    print(f"   {metric}: {value:.4f}")
                else:
                    print(f"   {metric}: {value}")

        # Signal other ranks that evaluation is complete
        if dist.is_initialized():
            dist.barrier()

        return metrics

    def _is_evaluation_completed(self, stage: str) -> bool:
        """Check if evaluation was completed for a stage by looking for test predictions file."""
        test_predictions_file = os.path.join(
            self.results_dir, stage, "results", "test_predictions.jsonl"
        )
        metrics_file = os.path.join(self.results_dir, stage, "results", "metrics.json")

        # Check if both files exist
        if not os.path.exists(test_predictions_file) or not os.path.exists(
            metrics_file
        ):
            return False

        # Also check if metrics file has evaluation results
        try:
            with open(metrics_file, "r") as f:
                metrics = json.load(f)
            return "test_loss" in metrics
        except:
            return False

## OpenTSLM audit and run recommendation

### Primary sources

- [OpenTSLM v3 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02410)
- [Official repository](https://github.com/OpenTSLM/OpenTSLM)
- [Repository at our pinned commit](https://github.com/OpenTSLM/OpenTSLM/tree/2968f4b891baab4307f7e9d0043e87677b593a30)
- [HAR SoftPrompt checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-1b-har-sp)
- [Project page](https://www.opentslm.com/)

### Architecture and suitability

Sourced facts:

- SoftPrompt independently patches each univariate series with a Conv1d whose kernel and stride equal 4.
- Each 4-sample patch becomes a 128-dimensional token, receives a learned positional embedding, passes through a six-layer Transformer encoder, then through LayerNorm → Linear → GELU into the Llama hidden dimension.
- The resulting soft tokens are interleaved with text descriptions and consumed by a frozen Llama backbone with trainable LoRA adapters.
- The autoregressive loss covers only generated answer tokens, including rationale and final answer.
- The scratch encoder supports at most 1,024 patches per series, or 4,096 samples at patch size 4.
- The paper notes SoftPrompt memory scales poorly with total time-series-token count; Flamingo is preferable for substantially longer/more multivariate contexts.

For Trace:

- Seven 1,024-sample channels become `7 × 256 = 1,792` time-series tokens, plus text and answer tokens.
- This is safely within Llama 3.2 1B’s context and the encoder’s positional limit, but about 18.7× HAR’s time-series-token load: HAR uses `3 × 128/4 = 96` tokens.
- Each channel is encoded independently. Cross-channel comparison happens only in Llama attention after projection; there is no joint multichannel encoder.
- Four-sample patches imply nominal 4 ms temporal granularity, but the architecture has no regression head. Onset is learned as integer text under ordinary next-token CE, so a 1 ms miss and a 400 ms miss receive no distance-aware distinction.
- Therefore the architecture is credible for natural-language QA and coarse localization, but weak joint attribution/localization are expected failure modes, not surprises.

### Paper curriculum and HAR-CoT

The paper describes two conceptual phases:

1. Encoder warm-up with TSQA multiple choice and M4 captioning.
2. CoT specialization with HAR, Sleep, and ECG datasets.

The official implementation exposes these operationally as five sequential stages and loads the previous stage’s best checkpoint. The HAR checkpoint is an appropriate warm start because HAR is multivariate sensor CoT, although its sparse model card only explicitly says it was trained on HAR; cumulative checkpoint lineage is inferred from the official curriculum code.

- descriptions and rationale text.

projector: 0.0001
lora: 0.00002

Use canonical, unaugmented validation only. Add a fixed generation panel stratified by:

- strongest joint, including every available J5–J7 example;
- onset-time quintile;
- event semantics.
